full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J: The Managing Director of an Export-oriented Garments Industry, the complainant opposite party No.2, Majedur Rahman lodged a complaint petition before the Chief Metro politan Magistrate, Dhaka being Petition Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 under sections 420/406/109 of the Penal Code against three foreigners named Mr G Franco Tacchinardi, and his two sons Mr Angelo Tacchinardi and Mr Paolo Tacchinardi, implicating them in the said petition case for the alleged offence of cheating and criminal misappropriation against which accused petitioner No.1 preferred this miscellaneous application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained this Rule on 23-1-2001 calling upon the State-opposite party and the complainant opposite party No. 2 to show cause as to why the proceeding in CR Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 pending in the Court of Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka should not be quashedand/or to pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may deem fit and proper. At the time of issuance of the Rule all further proceeding in CR Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 pending as aforesaid has been stayed by this Court. 

 3. The learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, after examining the complainant opposite party No.2 under the provision of section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, issued process against the accused petitioner and two others pursuant to which the accused persons appeared before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and obtained enlargement on bail from the said court. Thereafter, the accused persons preferred an application under section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, praying to discharge them from the case, but the Court after rejecting the said application, framed charge against the accused petitioner and two others under section 420/406 of the Penal Code. 

 4. Challenging the entire proceeding in Petition Case No. 1687(A) of 1999, the accused petitioner No. 1 preferred this miscellaneous application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained the instant Rule. 

 6. Mr Md Badruddoza, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused petitioner, at the very outset, has taken us through the entire statement made in the complaint petition, Annexure-A appended to the miscellaneous application and strenuously argued that from the facts stated in the comaint petition it reveals clearly that the entire allegation s raised against the accused petitioner and his two sons is based on preposterous facts in as much as the affairs of the export of garments by the complainant opposite party No.2 to his foreign buyer is guided and regulated under the provision of Uniform Customs and Practice for documentary credit, (UCP), 1993 revision, adopted by the International Chamber of Commerce, (ICC) to which Bangladesh is also a Member, and published through the ICC publication No. 500 and as such, the statement regarding the execution of an undertaking by the accused petitioners concerning the commitment of the payment of the Bill involved in the International Documentary Credit by the accused petitioner and two others, being contrary to the provision of International Trading Practice is a palpably falsehood Mr Badruddoza next submits that the statement made in the complaint petition not only admitted the fact, but also revealed, that business transactions have been in existence between the complainant opposite party and the foreign buyer Messrs Oscon Textile Ltd. and, as such, these called nonpayment of dues in part of the letter of credit by the foreign buyer being an admitted business transaction cannot be treated as a commission of offence under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code. The learned Advocate Mr Badruddoza further submits that the requirement of an element as to initial deception for constituting offence under section 420 of the Penal Code having been absent in the statement of the complaint petition regarding alleged commission of offence, the proceeding as initiated under section 420 of the Penal Code cannot be maintained against the accused petitioner and two others. Mr Badruddoza categorically argued that section 406 of the Penal Code since provided for punishment for the misappropriation of property which was alleged to have been within the domain of the accused petitioner. The same cannot be maintained against the accused petitioner and his two sons since admittedly, they did not misappropriate any entrustment of any property owned by the complainant opposite party No. 2. Mr Badruddoza finally submits that no allegation of criminal offence since present in the complaint petition and since the element of offence under sections 420 and 406 is absent in the statement of the complaint petition and since the entire allegation brought against the accused petitioner is based on preposterous facts, the proceeding in CR No. 1687(A) of 1999, now pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against the accused petitioner and two others is an abuse of the process of the court and, as such, liable to be interfered with and quashed by this court. Mr Badruddoza, in this context, heavily relied on the case of Dewan Obaidur Rahman vs State reported in 1999 BLD (AD) 128 = 4 BLC (AD) 167. Mr Badruddoza also referred through the provision of Uniform Customs and Practice for documentary credit, (UCP), 1993 revision published though the ICC Publication No. 500 in order to show the practice and procedure regarding International Documents Credit prevailing currently. In support of his contention regarding UCP for documentary credit, the learned Advocate referred the case of Korea Exchange Bank, Seoul, Korea vs Gemini Garments Limited and others reported in 1 LQ (2004) 276 = 56 DLR 392. 

 7. On the other hand, the learned Assistant Attorney-General Ms. Shamim Ara Dora finds it difficult to oppose the Rule in view of the referred decision which aptly attracts to this case. 

 8. We have perused the miscellaneous application along with annexure appended thereto, specially the complaint petition, and considered the arguments advanced at the Bar. 

 9. The complainant opposite party No. 2 in the complaint petition categorically stated that he was supplying garments from his Export Oriented Garment Industry Messrs Millan Apparels Ltd to the foreign buyers Messrs Oscon Textile Ltd. in Italy under business agreement since 1985 and. the accused petitioner and his two sons namely, Mr Angelo Tacchinardi and Mr Paolo Tacchinardi were the representatives from his foreign buyer sent to Bangladesh for the purpose of the inspection and certification as to the quality of the manufactured garments. It has been further stated in the complaint petition that the business transaction started in the year 1985 continued for 12 years without any dispute between the parties and the complainant opposite party No. 2 received the payment of the letter of credit opened by the foreign buyers in all these years without any hindrance from them in any manner. The complainant opposite party No. 2 further stated that at a later stage when the complainant opposite party No.2 supplied a consignment ofgarments amounting to US$ 13,57,927.16 the dispute .arose from that point when .the letter of credit issuing bank sent a discrepancy notice to the complainant opposite party No. 2. Thereafter, the complainant opposite party No. 2 did not receive any payment from the foreign buyer and it further appeared to the complainant opposite party No. 2that the accused petitioner failed to comply with the undertaking they have executed that they will pay the letter of credit amount upon the failure of the foreign buyer to pay the foreign bill amount. He also complained that the accused persons created forged settlement papers showing that the bill has been settled between the parties. The complainant opposite party No. 2 treating this failure of the accused petitioner and non receipt of the letter of credit amount as a commission of offence under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code initiated the Complaint Case No. 1687 (A) of 1999 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against the accused petitioner and his two sons. The very statement of the complaint petition clearly evidenced that a long standing business transaction has been on existence between the complainant opposite party No. 2 and his foreign buyers Messrs Oscon Textile Limited which has been represented by the accused petitioner and two others. It transpires that the transaction made between the parties has been through the international documentary credit meaning as made through the letter of credit under the bank channel. It appears from the ICC Publication No. 500 that International Documentary Credit is currently guided and regulated by the provision of Uniform Custom and Practice for Documentary Credit, (UCP), 1993 revision, published. by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) Publication No. 500 which is recognised universally by 150 countries including Bangladesh. Upon perusing a copy of ICC 500, as submitted by Mr Badruddoza, it transpires that out of four parties involved in the international documentary credit, the foreign buyer being the "applicant for the credit" before the letter of credit "Issuing Bank" in his country establishes letter of credit making the supplier as "Beneficiary" of the credit, undertakes to pay the amount under the credit both against "issuing" and "correspondent" Bank. Practically, this issuing bank gives an undertaking, as principal, to pay against correct documents in accordance with the mandate of the buyer. The seller, being the beneficiary of the international documentary credit, is liable, under the provision of UCP, 1993 revision, ICC Publication No.500 to .present correct documents before the issuing Bank, else the issuing bank shall not be liable to pay under the documents as the doctrine of strict compliance is fundamental to the operation of letters of credit. 

 10. In the case of Korea Exchange Bank, Seoul, Korea vs Gemini Garments Limited and others reported in 2004 LG 276 his Lordship Mr Justice Mohammad Abdur Rashid sitting in a Division Bench of this Court has examined the Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit, 1983 revision. ICC Publication No.400, which is the previous version of ICC Publication No. 500, on the question of liability of the parties regarding the payment of letter of credit and held as under: 

 "In summarising, we are of the view that an irrevocable letter of credit constitutes a definite undertaking of the issuing bank, which it must honour and pay according to the terms and conditions of the credit. It is not concerned. in the least with any dispute between the seller and buyer for any breach of the contract underlying the letter of credit. It is however, obliged to refuse payment when there is a clear fraud of which it has notice or knowledge. The court shall not interfere with such irrevocable/confirmed commitment of such bank except in case of clear or established fraud or in cases of irretrievable injustice or special equities. 

 11. From the above provision of UCP, 1993 revision, ICC Publication No. 500 there appears no scope for any individual other than those four parties involved in the credit, to undertake to pay under the International Documentary Credit or to make any out of channel amicable settlement as to the payment of foreign bill. That being the mandatory practice followed in the foreign trading and the complainant opposite party No.2 being in acquaintance with the practice, at least for admittedly 12 years, the execution of any private undertaking regarding payment of International bill by the accused petitioner and two others and placing reliance upon such undertaking by the complainant opposite party No. 2 is a story contrary to the provision of law and, as such, so preposterous that it cannot be believed as a true statement of facts. A statement of facts is preposterous if it is unreasonable, especially in a way that is silly under the facts and circumstances of the entire case. The way the complainant opposite party No. 2 brought the allegation of cheating and criminal misappropriation against the accused petitioner and his two sons, who are foreigners and present in Bangladesh for the purpose of representing a foreign buyer is shocking, unreasonable, annoying and so silly that it can be treated in no manner other than as preposterous facts. The learned Advocate Mr Md Badruddoza, in this context, strenuously argued that such a preposterous story, as stated in the complaint petition, being the basis of the entire allegation against the accused petitioner and two others, the proceeding in Petition Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 is an abuse of the process of the Court and, as such, the same cannot be maintained against the accused petitioner and two others. 

 12. We are in agreement with the learned Advocate Mr Badruddoza since the statements made in the complaint petition being contrary to the provision of International Practice, is preposterous one so as to treat the entire proceeding in Petition Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 as an abuse of the process of the Court. 

 13. Now, turning to the point that the transaction made between the parties being a business transaction whether covered through the decision of the apex court, we have considered' the referred decision of the case of Dewan Obaidur Rahman vs State reported in 1999 J3LD (AD) 128 =4 BLC (AD) 167 in which their Lordships in the Appellate Division held as under; 

 14. From the aforesaid decision it appears that by the time now it became an established principle that non payment of dues under business transaction cannot be treated as a commission of offence under sections 406 and 420 of the Penal Code. Since the entire statements made in the complaint pennon clearly revealed that the allegation as raised by the complainant opposite party No.2 is based upon the business transaction, we have no hesitation but to hold that the entire proceeding in CR Case No. 1687 (A) on 999 cannot be maintained since the same is an abuse of the process of the court. 

 16. In the case of Abdur Rhman alias Bablu vs Santosh Kumar Shadhu and another reported in 46 DLR (AD) 180 their Lordship in the Appellate Division, on the question of requirement of the statement of initial deception, held as follows: 

 21. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The proceeding in CR Case No. 1687(A) of 1999 under sections 420/406 of the Penal Code pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against the accused petitioner and two others is hereby quashed.
